entry:
Diverse group of photosynthetic organisms that excludes the land plants. Algae range from microscopic unicellular microalgae, including [[Cyanobacteria|cyanobacteria]] and phytoplankton, to [[Seaweed|seaweeds]], multicellular macroalgae that may grow up to 50 m (160 ft) in length. Most are aquatic, especially marine, and most are [[Plankton|plankton]] carried passively by water. Freshwater forms include [[Charophyta]] such as the filamentous *Spirogyra*. Most algae are single-celled and lack roots, leaves, or stems.

Algae are polyphyletic, having multiple evolutionary origins. Chlorophytes, [[Red algae|red algae]], and glaucophytes have primary chloroplasts derived directly from endosymbiont cyanobacteria, while [[Diatom|diatoms]], euglenoids, and brown algae have secondary chloroplasts derived indirectly from endosymbiont red or green algae. Algae contain chlorophyll a as their primary photosynthetic pigment, and their photosynthetic machinery, ultimately derived from cyanobacteria, produces oxygen by splitting water molecules. Most are photoautotrophs and the main primary producers of aquatic ecosystems; some are mixotrophs, and some unicellular algae are heterotrophs or parasites. Oceanic phytoplankton generate roughly half of Earth's atmospheric oxygen. Fossilized filamentous algae from the Vindhya basin have been dated to 1.6 to 1.7 billion years ago. Only the reds, browns, and some chlorophytes form three-dimensional multicellular bodies; the brown [[Kelp|kelps]] reach 50 m. Certain species form harmful blooms that deplete oxygen and release toxins.

Seaweed farming has existed for thousands of years and is strongly rooted in East Asian food cultures. Modern uses include cattle feed, bioremediation, algae fuels, and medical and scientific applications. The study of algae is called phycology.

Branch of mathematics that studies abstract systems, known as [[Algebraic structure|algebraic structures]], and the manipulation of expressions within those systems. Algebra generalizes [[Arithmetic|arithmetic]] by introducing variables and algebraic operations other than the standard arithmetic operations, such as addition and multiplication.

An algebraic structure is a non-empty set of mathematical objects, such as the integers, together with operations defined on that set. Arithmetic studies operations in a particular domain of numbers, such as the real numbers. Elementary algebra is the first level of abstraction above it; abstract algebra is a higher level, not limited to a particular domain; and universal algebra is more abstract still, investigating the characteristics of algebraic structures in general.

[[Elementary algebra]], also called school algebra, is the oldest and most basic form. It uses [[Variable (mathematics)|variables]], symbols for unspecified or unknown quantities, to express general laws, such as the commutative property of multiplication, a × b = b × a. Algebraic expressions combine variables and numbers, as in 5x + 3. An equation states that two expressions are equal. Identity equations, such as 2x + 5x = 7x, are true for all values of the variables; conditional equations are true only for some values, as x² = 4 is true if x is either 2 or −2. Elementary algebra seeks the values for which a statement is true by transforming equations to isolate variables. [[Linear algebra]] is a closely related field that investigates linear equations and systems of them, and supports applications in data analysis and quantum mechanics.

[[Abstract algebra]] studies algebraic structures, which consist of a set of objects with one or several operations. It allows objects other than numbers and non-arithmetic operations, and distinguishes types of structures, such as groups, rings, and fields, by the number of operations they use and the laws, called axioms, they follow. Universal algebra and category theory provide general frameworks for studying classes of structures.

Algebraic methods were first studied in the ancient period to solve specific problems in fields like geometry; Babylonian clay tablets from around 1800 BC solved quadratic equations by geometric methods. [[Brahmagupta]] established rules for zero, negative quantities, and operations on variables. In the 9th century the Persian mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa [[Al-Khwarizmi|al-Khwarizmi]] systematized algebra as an independent discipline, distinct from geometry. The word comes from the Arabic *al-jabr*, which originally referred to bonesetting; he used it in the title of his treatise *The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing*. The word entered English in the 16th century. Equations were described in words and abbreviations until the 16th and 17th centuries, when a rigorous symbolic formalism developed. In the mid-19th century algebra broadened beyond a theory of equations to cover diverse operations and structures. It is relevant to geometry, topology, number theory, calculus, logic, physics, and computer science.

Country in the Maghreb region of North Africa; capital and largest city, [[Algiers]]. Officially the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria, it borders Tunisia, Libya, Niger, Mali, Mauritania, Western Sahara, Morocco, and the Mediterranean Sea. It spans 2,381,741 sq km (919,595 sq mi), the largest area of any African country, and has a population of 47 million, concentrated in the fertile, mountainous north; the [[Sahara]] covers most of the country. Official languages are Arabic and Amazigh, though most people speak Algerian Arabic. Most Algerians identify as Arabs, with [[Berbers]] a sizeable minority. Sunni Islam is the official religion and is practiced by 99% of the population.

Indigenous Amazigh societies, including the Numidians, shaped early Algeria, along with Phoenician, Roman, Vandal, and Byzantine influences. From the 7th century Islam and Arab tribes transformed the region, and local Islamic dynasties ruled between the 8th and 15th centuries. The Regency of Algiers, established in 1516, owed nominal allegiance to the [[Ottoman Empire]]. France invaded in 1830, annexed the country in 1848, and did not fully conquer it until 1903. Resistance ranged from [[Emir Abdelkader|Emir Abdelkader's]] campaigns to 20th-century nationalism and the [[Algerian War]], which began in 1954. Algeria became independent in 1962. A civil war ran from 1992 to 2002, and a state of emergency lasted until the 2010–2012 protests. Further protests, the Hirak, took place in 2019–2021.

Algeria is a semi-presidential republic; critics cite strong military influence and restrictions on dissent. It has the highest [[Human Development Index]] in continental Africa, the third-largest economy in Africa, and the continent's largest military budget. Hydrocarbons account for roughly 30% of GDP, 60% of budget revenues, and nearly 95% of exports.

Finite sequence of rigorous instructions, used in mathematics and [[Computer science|computer science]] to solve a class of problems or perform a computation. More advanced algorithms use conditionals to route execution along different paths (automated decision-making) and deduce valid inferences (automated reasoning).

An algorithm can be expressed in a finite amount of space and time and in a well-defined formal language. Starting from an initial state and input, which may be empty, the instructions proceed through a finite number of well-defined states, eventually producing output and terminating. Transitions are not necessarily deterministic; randomized algorithms incorporate random input. By contrast, a [[Heuristic|heuristic]] is a problem-solving approach that may not guarantee correct or optimal results. A program is an algorithm only if it stops eventually. In *The Art of Computer Programming*, [[Donald Knuth]] specified five properties: finiteness, definiteness, input, output, and effectiveness. Efficiency, measured by time and space complexity, affects performance: mergesort scales as O(n log n), far better than simpler quadratic-time alternatives.

Step-by-step procedures are recorded in Babylonian mathematics (around 2500 BC), Egyptian mathematics (around 1550 BC), and Indian, Greek, Chinese, and Arabic mathematics. A Sumerian tablet from Shuruppak, c. 2500 BC, describes the earliest division algorithm. The [[Euclidean algorithm]] was first described in Euclid's *Elements* (c. 300 BC), and the [[Sieve of Eratosthenes]] in Nicomachus's *Introduction to Arithmetic*. In the 9th century [[Al-Kindi]] gave the first description of cryptanalysis by frequency analysis, the earliest codebreaking algorithm.

The word derives from the Latinized name of the Persian scholar [[Al-Khwarizmi|al-Khwarizmi]], who around 825 AD wrote a book on Indian computation; its 12th-century Latin translations began *Dixit Algoritmi*, "Thus spoke Al-Khwarizmi." In English, *algorism* meant place-value calculation and occurs c. 1225; [[Geoffrey Chaucer|Chaucer]] used a variant in the late 14th century. Under the influence of Greek *arithmos*, "number," the Latin became *algorithmus* in the 15th century, and Thomas Hood used *algorithm* in English by 1596.

Fourth Rashidun caliph (r. 656–661) and first [[Shia Islam|Shia]] Imam, cousin and son-in-law of the prophet [[Muhammad]]. Born to Abu Talib and Fatima bint Asad, Ali was raised in Muhammad's household and was among the first to accept his teachings; the earliest sources place him before [[Abu Bakr]], though the order is debated among Shia and Sunni scholars. In 622 he stayed behind in Mecca as Muhammad's decoy when Muhammad escaped to Medina, where Muhammad swore a pact of brotherhood with him and gave him his daughter [[Fatima]] in marriage. Ali served as Muhammad's secretary and deputy and as flag-bearer of his army.

The meaning of Muhammad's statement at Ghadir Khumm in 632, "Whoever I am his mawla, then Ali is his mawla," is disputed. Shia Muslims hold that it invested Ali with Muhammad's religious and political authority; Sunni Muslims regard it as a statement of friendship. After Muhammad died in 632, a group of Muslims met in Ali's absence and appointed Abu Bakr as leader. Ali withdrew from public life under Abu Bakr and [[Umar]], then criticized [[Uthman]] while also mediating between the caliph and provincial dissidents.

After Uthman was assassinated in 656, the people of Medina urged Ali to lead, and after initial hesitation he accepted. Talha, Zubayr, and Muhammad's widow [[Aisha]], who sought to avenge Uthman, were defeated at the Battle of the Camel in 656. Mu'awiya fought him at the inconclusive Battle of Siffin in 657, and the ensuing arbitration alienated the Kharijites, whom Ali crushed at Nahrawan in 658. In 661, during Ramadan, the Kharijite Ibn Muljam assassinated him. His son Hasan abdicated that year, and Mu'awiya founded the [[Umayyad Caliphate]].

Sunni Muslims regard Ali as the last of the rightly guided caliphs; Shia Muslims venerate him as the first Imam and rightful successor to Muhammad. His shrine in Najaf, Iraq, is a major Shia pilgrimage destination, and his legacy is collected in *Nahj al-balagha*.

Exaggerated immune response in which the body mistakenly identifies an ordinarily harmless substance, the allergen, as a threat. Allergic reactions give rise to hay fever, allergic conjunctivitis, allergic [[Asthma|asthma]], [[Atopic dermatitis|atopic dermatitis]], food allergies, and anaphylaxis. Symptoms include red eyes, an itchy rash, sneezing, coughing, a runny nose, shortness of breath, or swelling. Common allergens include [[Pollen|pollen]], certain foods, metals, insect stings, medications, and latex.

Allergies develop through genetic and environmental factors. In the reaction, immunoglobulin E antibodies (IgE) bind to an allergen and then to a receptor on mast cells or basophils, which release inflammatory chemicals such as histamine. Insect stings, foods, and medicines such as [[Aspirin|aspirin]] and [[Penicillin|penicillin]] can produce anaphylaxis, a systemic reaction that may affect the skin, digestive, respiratory, and circulatory systems and can include low blood pressure, coma, and death. It may be sudden or delayed and may recur after seeming to subside.

Diagnosis is typically based on medical history. Skin or blood tests may help, but positive results do not necessarily indicate a significant allergy. Treatment includes avoiding known allergens and using medications such as steroids and antihistamines. Severe reactions call for injectable [[Adrenaline|adrenaline]] (epinephrine). Allergen immunotherapy, which gradually exposes people to larger amounts of allergen, is useful for some allergies, such as hay fever and reactions to insect bites; its use in food allergy is unclear. Early exposure of children to potential allergens may be protective.

In the developed world about 20% of people are affected by allergic rhinitis, food allergy affects 10% of adults and 8% of children, and about 20% have or have had atopic dermatitis. Depending on the country, about 1–18% of people have asthma, and anaphylaxis occurs in 0.05–2%. Rates of many allergic diseases appear to be increasing. Clemens von Pirquet first used the word "allergy" in 1906.

Mixture of chemical elements, in most cases at least one of them metallic, that retains the characteristics of a metal. Alloys often have properties that differ from those of their constituents. Most metals used commercially are alloyed to improve strength, hardness, or corrosion resistance, or to lower cost, as in alloys of gold and copper. Atoms in an alloy are joined by [[Metallic bonding|metallic bonding]] rather than the covalent bonds typical of chemical compounds. Constituents are usually measured by mass percentage in practice and by atomic fraction in basic science.

Alloys are classified as substitutional or interstitial by atomic arrangement, and as homogeneous (a single phase), heterogeneous (two or more phases), or intermetallic. An alloy may be a solid solution in which all crystals have the same composition, or a mixture of phases forming a microstructure of different crystals. Each constituent has a saturation point: iron can hold at most 6.67% carbon, forming cementite.

Alloying changes mechanical behavior. Soft aluminium becomes much stronger when alloyed with copper. Adding a small amount of carbon to iron trades ductility for strength, producing [[Steel|steel]]; adding chromium raises corrosion resistance, producing [[Stainless steel|stainless steel]]. Other examples include red gold (gold and copper), white gold (gold and silver), sterling silver (silver and copper), solder, brass, pewter, and duralumin. Alloys serve in uses from buildings and surgical tools to titanium alloys in aerospace and beryllium-copper alloys for non-sparking tools.

Some alloys occur naturally, such as [[Electrum|electrum]], of silver and gold; meteorites are sometimes made of natural iron-nickel alloys. [[Bronze]], of tin and copper, was one of the first alloys made by humans and is much stronger and harder than either component. In ancient times steel could arise only as an accidental byproduct of smelting iron ore. Most alloys, including various aluminium, titanium, nickel, and magnesium alloys, were not created until the 1900s.

[[Writing system]] that uses a standard set of symbols, called graphemes or letters, to represent more or less the sounds of a spoken language. These graphemes largely correspond to [[Phoneme|phonemes]], the smallest sound segments that distinguish one word from another. A syllabary, by contrast, assigns symbols to syllables, and logographies assign symbols to words, morphemes, or other semantic units. Peter T. Daniels distinguishes true alphabets, which use letters for both consonants and vowels, from abjads, which generally lack vowel indicators, and abugidas, which mark vowels with diacritics. In this narrower sense the Greek alphabet was the first true alphabet; it derived from the Phoenician alphabet, an abjad.

The first letters were invented in Ancient Egypt to aid in writing [[Egyptian hieroglyphs]]. About 24 hieroglyphs, the uniliterals, gave single sounds; the system was used until the 5th century AD. A script appeared in Egyptian turquoise mines on the Sinai Peninsula c. 1840 BC, apparently left by Canaanite workers, and an earlier version dated to c. 1800 BC was found at Wadi el-Hol in 1999. This Proto-Sinaitic script had no vowel characters. The best-attested Bronze Age alphabet is Ugaritic, an alphabetic cuneiform script of 30 signs invented in [[Ugarit]] before the 15th century BC.

Proto-Sinaitic developed into the [[Phoenician alphabet]] before c. 1050 BC. The oldest Phoenician text is an inscription on the sarcophagus of King Ahiram, c. 1000 BC. With only about two dozen letters, it was simple enough for trade, and it is the ultimate ancestor of many modern scripts, including Arabic, Cyrillic, Greek, Hebrew, and Latin. Aramaic gave rise to the [[Hebrew alphabet]].

Alphabets usually have a standard order, which allows alphabetical sorting and the use of letters to number items. The word comes from Late Latin *alphabetum* and Greek *alphabētos*, made from *alpha* and *beta*, which in turn came from Phoenician *aleph*, "ox," and *bet*, "house."

River, northern South America, the largest in the world by discharge volume of water. Its length is recognized as 6,400 km (4,000 mi), though reports range from 6,575 to 7,062 km (4,086 to 4,388 mi), and whether it or the [[Nile]] is the longest river system is disputed. A 2014 study found its farthest source to be the headwaters of the Mantaro River in Peru, replacing the Apurímac River's headwaters on Nevado Mismi. The Mantaro and Apurímac join with other tributaries to form the Ucayali, which meets the Marañón upstream of Iquitos; countries other than [[Brazil]] regard this as the main stem. Brazilians call the section above the confluence with the [[Rio Negro (Amazon)|Rio Negro]] the Solimões, and the river below it, from the Meeting of Waters at [[Manaus]], the Amazon.

Average discharge is about 215,000 to 230,000 cubic meters per second, greater than the next seven largest independent rivers combined and 20% of global riverine discharge into oceans. Its basin, the largest in the world, covers approximately 7,000,000 sq km (2,700,000 sq mi) and contains the [[Amazon rainforest]]. The river carries sediment averaging nearly 600 million tons annually to the [[Atlantic Ocean]].

Geological studies suggest that for millions of years the river flowed east to west, until the rising [[Andes]] blocked its flow to the Pacific. It became Rio Amazonas after native warriors, led by women, attacked a 16th-century expedition under Francisco de Orellana, recalling the Amazon warriors of Greek mythology.

Archaeological evidence shows complex, large-scale indigenous societies, mainly chiefdoms with towns and cities. Archaeologists estimate that more than 3 million indigenous people lived around the river when Orellana traveled it in 1541, and the island of [[Marajó]] may have supported 100,000. Repeated burning enriched soils into dark earth known as *terra preta*, which supported large-scale agriculture.

Moist broadleaf [[Tropical rainforest|tropical rainforest]] that covers most of the Amazon basin of South America. The basin encompasses 7 million sq km (2.7 million sq mi), of which 6 million sq km (2.3 million sq mi) are rainforest, spanning nine nations and 3,344 indigenous territories. Sixty percent of the forest lies in [[Brazil]], 13% in [[Peru]], and 10% in [[Colombia]], with smaller portions in six other countries. It is more than half of the world's remaining rainforest and the largest and most biodiverse tract of tropical rainforest, with an estimated 390 billion trees in about 16,000 species. It regulates regional climate through transpiration-driven rainfall and stores large quantities of carbon, though deforestation and warming have caused portions to shift from net carbon sinks to sources.

More than 30 million people of 350 ethnic groups live there; [[Indigenous peoples]] make up 9% of the population, and 60 groups remain largely isolated. Excavation at Caverna da Pedra Pintada shows humans settled the region at least 11,200 years ago. Archaeologist Betty Meggers argued that poor soil could not support a large population, but later findings suggest dense settlement. Some 5 million people may have lived in the region in AD 1500; the native population fell to 1 million by 1900 and below 200,000 by the early 1980s, and disease, including smallpox, is believed to have devastated earlier civilization. Francisco de Orellana was the first European to travel the length of the [[Amazon River]], in 1542. Since the 1970s numerous geoglyphs dating from AD 1–1250 have been found on deforested land, and *terra preta*, a fertile soil, is widely accepted as a product of indigenous soil management.

Large-scale [[Deforestation|deforestation]], driven by soy, cattle ranching, mining, and logging, has caused cumulative losses approaching 20% of the original forest cover. Annual rates in Brazil fell by nearly 50% in the first ten months of 2023 compared with 2022. In 2023 the World Bank published a report proposing a non-deforestation economic program for the region.
